title: Generative AI and the future of higher education: a threat to academic integrity or reformation? Evidence from multicultural perspectives
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI (GenAI) is being used and perceived in higher education, with a particular focus on multicultural differences. The authors argue that although GenAI has been widely discussed in education, prior work has not sufficiently examined how views about its benefits, risks, ethics, and regulation vary across cultural contexts. The study therefore asks four main questions: levels of awareness and familiarity with GenAI, extent of use across cultures, perceived benefits and concerns, and opinions about needed policies and ethical regulations.

The study uses an embedded mixed-methods design centered on an online survey. Quantitative data were the primary component, supplemented by qualitative open-ended responses. The survey collected 1,217 valid responses from students and lecturers in higher education institutions across 76 countries, recruited through social media, academic forums, mailing lists, and research platforms. Participants represented diverse genders, academic roles, disciplines, and locations. The survey measured awareness, familiarity, use, perceived cheating/plagiarism, perceived benefits and concerns, and views on regulation. The authors also linked responses to Hofstede cultural dimensions to analyze associations between cultural context and attitudes toward GenAI.

Findings showed high awareness of GenAI, especially ChatGPT, and substantial prior use, with many respondents intending to continue using such tools. The most common uses were information retrieval and text paraphrasing, followed by self-learning, assignments, writing support, and recreation. Respondents generally saw GenAI as useful for answering questions, supporting personalized learning, brainstorming, literature search, writing assistance, and improving educational access. At the same time, they expressed strong concerns about factual inaccuracy, contextual inappropriateness, bias, overreliance, plagiarism, and threats to academic integrity.

The paper concludes that GenAI has meaningful potential in higher education, but its responsible integration requires strong ethical guidance and policy development. Cultural dimensions—especially uncertainty avoidance and long-term orientation—were associated with differences in perceived benefits, concerns, and whether GenAI use was viewed as cheating. The authors argue that GenAI should not simply be banned or adopted uncritically; instead, higher education institutions should develop culturally responsive policies that encourage productive use while addressing academic integrity, fairness, and ethical risks.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools broadly, including text- and media-generating systems used for conversational assistance, paraphrasing, writing support, information retrieval, and related academic tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied via a multicultural survey of higher-education students and teachers about awareness, familiarity, usage, perceived benefits, concerns, cheating/plagiarism, and policy preferences regarding generative AI tools in higher education.

findings.finding_summary: Across 1,217 higher-education participants from 76 countries, respondents reported high awareness of GenAI tools (81.76%). Reported uses centered on information retrieval (44.3%), text paraphrasing (39.4%), recreation (31.4%), assignments (29.8%), self-learning (28.5%), written content generation (27.2%), and conversation (23.3%), indicating substantial operational and academic uptake. Participants also agreed that GenAI can respond to questions easily (M=4.302, SD=0.891), provide personalized and immediate learning support (M=4.082, SD=0.961), and support knowledge acquisition and writing tasks (M=4.016, SD=0.968).
findings.measure: Survey responses on awareness, use frequency/purpose, and perceived benefits (Likert means)

findings.finding_summary: Participants expressed generally positive but qualified views of GenAI’s educational value. They agreed that GenAI supports brainstorming (M=3.837, SD=1.080), literature search and summarized reading (M=3.783, SD=1.201), and equity/access (M=3.801, SD=1.037), but were neutral on whether it promotes creativity and critical thinking (M=3.327, SD=1.373), helps solve problems beyond the teacher’s scope (M=3.255, SD=1.207), or can reform education (M=3.382, SD=1.204).
findings.measure: Perceived educational potential of GenAI on Likert-scale survey items

findings.finding_summary: Respondents reported substantial academic-integrity concerns around GenAI. They agreed that GenAI can generate factually inaccurate output (M=4.181, SD=1.021), out-of-context or inappropriate output (M=3.984, SD=1.127), promote cheating and plagiarism (M=4.002, SD=1.108), hinder student/teacher growth through over-reliance (M=4.037, SD=1.119), and threaten academic integrity (M=3.807, SD=1.258). In direct classification items, 46.4% viewed student use of GenAI for academic work as cheating and 45.4% said the same for teacher academic work.
findings.measure: Survey items on concerns, cheating/plagiarism perceptions, and academic-integrity threat

findings.finding_summary: Cultural dimensions were significantly associated with GenAI attitudes. High uncertainty-avoidance cultures were more likely to classify student use of GenAI as cheating (OR=3.671, 95% CI [1.56–3.68], p<0.001), and long-term-oriented cultures were also more likely to do so (OR=2.870, CI [1.76–3.98], p<0.01). Uncertainty avoidance was negatively correlated with perceived GenAI potential (r=-0.375, p<0.01) and positively correlated with concerns (r=0.539, p<0.001), while long-term orientation was positively associated with perceived potential (r=0.272, p<0.05).
findings.measure: Ordinal logistic regression and correlation between Hofstede cultural dimensions and GenAI attitudes

findings.finding_summary: Policy views showed demand for regulation alongside continued use. 42.7% supported educational policies regulating GenAI in higher education, 22.4% opposed such policies, and 13.1% were unsure; qualitative responses most often favored restricting GenAI to self-learning, preventing use for assignments and research, and applying strict penalties for cheating/plagiarism. At the same time, 35.7% were very likely and 27.9% likely to continue using GenAI in the future.
findings.measure: Survey items and qualitative responses on regulation and future use intentions

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical mixed-methods survey study with descriptive, correlational, and qualitative analyses across a large international sample, but it is not an RCT, QED, or meta-analysis and does not estimate causal effects on learning outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports substantial perceptions of both benefits and risks, plus correlations with cultural dimensions, but no causal intervention effect sizes on student learning outcomes are provided, so impact remains unclear.
